t: Expanding Your Options

t: The Long-Term Memory Problem: Why Teaching and Learning Policies Fail 14, 2025
q: I quietly ask a student if I can borrow their exercise book. I leaf back to a lesson from three weeks ago, and ask the student a couple of basic recall questions about that lesson’s content. They cannot answer the questions.

However well designed our lessons, however clear our explanations, however thorough our checks for understanding and however extensive our independent practice: without a clear strategy for how students are going to remember it over the long term, we are wasting our time.

Professor Coe’s seminal work on “proxies for learning” taught us that when trying to establish the quality of a teacher or lesson we latch onto things that are readily observable, like student behaviour, busy-ness, and if feedback is being delivered.
When teachers “set and forget” they therefore communicate that they don’t really care what students do, so long as they do it. But if the teacher doesn’t care, the students certainly won’t.

t: Research Review: AI+Human Tutors Match Quality of Human-Only Tutors?
q: The researchers embedded three kinds of support inside Eedi, a math software platform. Support #1: Static pre-written hints. Support #2: A chat interface for accessing support from a human. Support #3: A chat interface for accessing support from an LLM, with a human approving the messages.
The study stored the original AI responses and the edits from human tutors (a fun source of data) which led to the finding that 76% of the LLM responses were accepted in full by the human tutor.
It's a small practical effect in a short intervention. The total time here was seven hours -- one hour per week over seven weeks -- for an increase of 5.5% on some proprietary measures.

It’s as if we asked Michael Bublé to play the kazoo and then supervise a robot purpose-built to play a kazoo. I’m not sure we’d be surprised by the results. I’m also not sure we’d feel good about saying “AI+Michael Bublé Match Quality Of Michael Bublé Alone.

It’s honestly quite strange to me that the Human + LLM showed its strengths with “Knowledge Transfer.” I would have expected to see the greatest difference on follow-up tasks that were closer to the tutoring moment.

I don’t hold up “time savings” as a first-order goal for teachers, administrators, or schools. There are plenty of ways to save time that result in a worse education for kids. But I am much more optimistic that AI can support back-office operational tasks like this rather than the in-classroom relational work of teaching.

t: Court Ruling A Roadblock To West Virginia Charter Schools
q: On December 3, Kanawha Circuit Judge Jennifer Bailey issued a permanent injunction that prevents the West Virginia Professional Charter School Board from authorizing any new charter schools without the approval of the voters in the county where the charter wants to do business.

West Virginia's constitution offers a clear statement about establishing new schools: No independent free school district, or organization shall hereafter be created, except with the consent of the school district or districts out of which the same is to be created, expressed by a majority of the voters voting on the question.

In 2021, the state modified the charter law. The bill turned every mention of 'charter school' into 'public charter school,' and it created the West Virginia Professional Charter School Board, a new path for charter authorization. The board members are appointed by the governor, and they had the power to authorize a charter school anywhere in the state, even if that charter had been previously rejected by the local elected school board.

The law was challenged in court in 2021 by Sam Brunett and Robert McCloud. Their lawsuit did not challenge the effectiveness of charter schools, but argued that the new approval process violated the state constitution.

t: Ask the Cognitive Scientist: What Do IQ Scores Mean?
a: Eric Turkheimer and Daniel T. Willingham
q: An IQ score is a summary of how successfully a child can answer the types of questions that are frequently posed in school, especially questions that require thinking abstractly with words, numbers, or space. This summary number is not meaningless because it predicts students’ success in school and in many jobs.
A better way to think about an IQ score is as a snapshot of achievement now, rather than future potential.

Binet intended his test as a diagnostic tool for children experiencing difficulties in school and did not use the term intelligence quotient (IQ). He was suspicious of attempts to boil the results of his measures down to a single number.

Intelligence tests are not measures of an essence. Intelligence tests measure people's tendency to give correct answers to questions... IQ tests are a description of the fact that some people are more accurate thinkers than others, not an explanation of why they are.

In a landmark 2018 paper, researchers analyzed studies using this method and two other research designs that enable researchers to estimate the impact of schooling on IQ. Combining the three methods, they concluded that attending school does make you smarter. By their reckoning, each additional year of education improves IQ between one and five points.

The researcher James Flynn analyzed the results of intelligence tests administered from the 1930s to the 1980s and found that average intelligence had increased by between 5 and 25 points per generation. These increases cannot possibly be genetic in origin.
With practice, training, and above all, method, we manage to increase our attention, our memory, our judgment, and literally to become more intelligent than we were before.

t: Your Brain Is Rotting: A Leadership Survival Guide
q: The human brain evolved for bursts of decision-making, not for 50+ decisions a day. It wasn't designed to handle a dozen tabs open, three simultaneous chat threads, constant notifications, and back-to-back Zoom meetings.

A study by McKinsey found that the average knowledge worker spends 62% of their time on “work about work”: meetings, email, coordination. Only 27% goes to actual skilled work, and a mere 11% to strategy or innovation. That's right. As a leader, you spend less than 3 hours a week on deep, creative, strategic thinking, the kind of thinking that moves your team forward.

When your brain is overloaded: Your memory fades. Your mood dips. You get reactive, not proactive. You avoid hard problems. You fall back on habits and familiar routines. Which means your leadership becomes… hollow.

You start to feel like a slightly worse version of yourself every week. It's not enough to crash, but just enough to coast. Until one day you wake up and realize: I haven't felt fully alive at work in months.

Most leaders don't recognize the problem, so they reach for the wrong fixes. … These are the equivalent of putting ice cubes in a burning room, hoping the room cools down. It won't. More tools won't save your brain from rotting. Less noise will.

I've found that the best ideas don't come when I'm sitting in front of my computer or browsing my phone. They come when my mind wanders. When I go for a walk (without my phone), in the shower, or when I'm lying down in bed. Studies from neuroscience (e.g., the DMN: Default Mode Network) show that the brain becomes more creative, reflective, and emotionally insightful when it's not focused on a task.
If an athlete ran 12 hours a day with no rest, what would you call him? Most will call him reckless. But when we, as leaders, run our brains to the extreme every week, we call it “drive.

Your edge as a leader isn't how much you do. It's how clearly you think. It's how calmly you decide. It's how creatively you solve problems. And none of that is possible if you allow your brain to rot under the noise and the pressure.” Archived from The Good Boss on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: When AI Becomes a Friend What High School AI Use Reveals
q: The headline numbers focus on companionship. In schools using AI minimally, 42% of students reported that they or a friend had used chatbots as companions. In schools using AI extensively, that number reached 59%. For romantic chatbot relationships, the gap was even wider: 9% versus 25%.” “Students in high-AI schools were also more likely to report using chatbots for mental health support (42% versus 63%), escaping from real life (42% versus 63%), and getting relationship advice (43% overall).

Teachers in high-AI schools were 56% more likely to report data breaches, more than twice as likely to hear about deepfake sexual imagery involving students, and nearly four times more likely to report AI systems failing to work as described.

Half of all students surveyed agreed that using AI in class makes them feel less connected to their teachers. In high-AI schools, that jumps to 56%. At the same time, these students are turning to AI more for companionship and emotional support.
One more detail: 31% of students who use AI chatbots for personal reasons do so on school-provided devices or software. The boundary between “school AI” and “personal AI” doesn't exist in practice.
When AI is everywhere at school, it becomes part of the landscape. Students don't naturally separate “school AI” from “personal AI” unless someone teaches them to.

Only 22% of students learned from their school when it's appropriate to use AI. Just 14% got guidance on what to do when AI gives problematic information. These gaps reflect how quickly this technology arrived, but they're gaps we can fill.

Students are already navigating AI relationships. Fifty-nine percent in high-AI schools report they or a friend use chatbots as companions. The question is whether they're doing this with knowledge and critical thinking that serves them well, or figuring it out alone.” Archived from Educating AI on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Using Knowledge-Building Curriculum Doesn't Guarantee 'Robust' Reading Comprehension
q: Robust” comprehension instruction, in contrast, might have students engage in some of those tasks, but the focus is on the overall meaning of the text. In other words, instead of using a text to teach a skill, a lesson that leads to robust comprehension puts the text in the foreground, bringing in whatever skills might help students understand and analyze that text.

According to a companion report from SRI, 47 percent of teachers said they modified half or more of a comprehension lesson, compared to only 13 percent who said they did so with a lesson in foundational reading skills like phonics. That report also found that many teachers viewed the comprehension aspect of their curriculum more difficult to implement, saying the texts were “too dense” and complex for their students.

Kristen McQuillan, a consultant who has worked with districts implementing knowledge-building curricula, says that from her observations, it's clear the curricula themselves aren't the reason so many lessons are surface-level. In many cases, she says, “teachers are changing the curriculum in pursuit of how to help kids master the standards.

One problem is that identifying character traits isn't a skill you can “master.” It will be easier or harder depending on the particular text. Another, McQuillan said, is that kids can get confused if the lesson objective is too “meta.

Like the state assessments, these tests present students with reading passages unrelated to anything they might have learned through the curriculum and provide teachers with data framed entirely in terms of the skills in literacy standards. They might tell teachers that students are weak in a skill like identifying the main idea of a text, when in fact the student might not have understood the text because of a lack of relevant background knowledge.

So while content-rich, knowledge-building curriculum doesn't guarantee robust instruction, it's crucial to enabling that kind of instruction to happen. Professional learning is also vital, for coaches and administrators as well as teachers.” Archived from Minding the Gap on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Point Game
q: My answer to this question in almost every context and for almost every student is the same; “Use The Point Game!” The Point Game is a cornerstone of Evidence-Based Literacy Instruction's (EBLI) approach to motivation and behavior reinforcement during instruction, whether in the whole class setting or 1:1.

Here's how it works: the instructor assigns a number of points for executing a particular skill independently, accurately, or correctly. If the student can demonstrate a skill, they earn X number of points. The teacher records their points in a T chart labeled Teacher v. Student.

Playing The Point Game presents an opportunity to build or break trust with students. Inevitably, you will be confronted with unexpected situations around earning points. In these moments, it is important to be honest about how many points you give for certain things and to demonstrate follow-through.

Taking away points is unnecessarily punitive, breaks trust with students, and complicates the mathematical function of The Point Game. Instead of taking away points, just give yourself points when the student does something that you want to reinforce against.

Give students the chance to earn large sums of points for hard tasks. Breaking a guessing habit, learning to use an “ice skater” finger underneath words while reading when they realllllllyyyy want to tap their finger across the page, keeping one's gaze fixed on a word while decoding instead of looking up at the teacher, these things are really difficult for students to implement, especially when it means fighting a strongly held habit.

Many teachers fall into the trap of never giving themselves any points, allowing the students points to stack up and surrendering, “you beat me, I didn't get a single one!” Over time, this will weaken the effectiveness of The Point Game because there is no real competition.

When I get points for students doing something they shouldn't, I clearly explain my rationale and then I give them a chance to try again, which might sound something like this; “I'm getting a point because you didn't form the letter F the way we practiced, with a hook around then cross. If you can do it right in the next word, you can get 5 points.

Wrap up each session by counting up the students points. This may be a moment to practice skip counting or multi-digit addition. It may be a moment to call out the hard work students did during the session, or remind them of something they learned and to practice those same strategies when reading independently.” Archived from Science of Reading Classroom on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Learning Science of Deep Processing
q: Shallow processing involves focusing on attributes that remain on the surface or the look-alike of what you want to learn (typically at the visual or sound levels), such as the appearance or pronunciation of words. It also refers to engaging in rote activities that reinforce those superficial aspects like repetition, rereading and highlighting.

Concentration is about attention. It's the ability to sustain focus and resist distraction. Deep processing is about what you do with that focus. You can concentrate intensely on a shallow task. Anyone who has ever memorized a list word for word knows this feeling. It takes effort. It feels demanding. And yet the information often disappears quickly.

A recent study showed that simply asking students “why?” after introducing new information made them remember that information incredibly better. The reason is elaborative interrogation: studies show that students who generate explanations remember more and transfer knowledge better than those who simply read explanations.

Research shows that relating information to yourself provides a powerful scaffold to organize information, not just emotional relevance. In practice, this means that tying information to personal experiences, goals or beliefs helps encoding by making it feel relevant to one's own life.

Short learning bursts feel faster, but they can slow down the path to durable understanding when they prevent deep engagement. Ironically, learners often reach long-term retention sooner by spending time processing meaning deeply than by spreading attention thin across many brief sessions.

Efficiency in learning is not necessarily about shorter exposure. It's about doing the right kind of thinking for the right amount of time and, paradoxically, that often means “for long enough”.” Archived from Kognitivo on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How to Think Like a Leader Before You Feel Like One
q: Early in my career I felt that credibility came from speed and execution. Clients asked a question; I raced to answer. Teams brought a problem; I offered a fix. As I took on leadership roles, I realised that (1) I didn't have time to be a doer in the same way; and (2) it was no longer my job to do so! Instead of acting and effectively closing spaces that others could own, I had to provide the space for others to think for themselves.

My natural instinct was (and still is!) to sketch a solution. Instead, I asked, “What would success look like if we got this right?” The room went quiet for a few seconds. Then, ideas started to surface: hesitant at first, then layered and richer. Within twenty minutes they had built a vision none of us could have produced alone.
Holding a question like in this example doesn't mean being evasive or lacking confidence. It means resisting the reflex to perform knowledge and instead creating a space for shared sense-making.

When I first stepped into leadership roles, I thought the job was to push. Push projects forward, push performance, push for change. It took me a while to realise that most people and teams actually struggle because something is slowing them down.

Leadership, I've learned, is often about identifying and removing these hidden barriers. You can spot them by paying attention to what hinders colleagues: unclear roles, competing expectations, unspoken conflict, fragmented processes, interpersonal tensions that people are worried they can't voice.

One of the hardest transitions in leadership is realising that your internal weather becomes everyone else's climate. You may think you're having a private moment of frustration, but people feel the shift instantly. Tone, posture, speed of speech — teams track these cues far more than we imagine.

My irritation didn't stay contained. It set the emotional baseline, and the meeting shifted toward managing the tension I had brought into the room. We spent the next hour dealing with the consequences of a mood swing rather than the substance of the work.

A leadership mindset is the craft of shaping the conditions under which good thinking, good work and good relationships can emerge. … Together, these practices shift leadership from performance to stewardship: you are not trying to be impressive, but to be useful.” Archived from Andrea Chiarelli on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How Do I Hold My People Accountable?
q: How do I hold my people accountable?” is the #1 question I get from the CEOs I teach. The answer is relatively simple, but it's not easy and it requires a pretty involved process.

The accountability process begins before you ever hire someone. It starts with you answering two questions: What job needs to be done? Who fits that role best? Making sure your hire has the right aptitude and motivation is critical. You can't hold someone accountable for work they don't have the skills to perform or the motivation to engage in.” “Once you've hired the right person, the next step in the accountability process is micro-training. Too many businesses skip this entirely, then act surprised when the new hire doesn't do things the way they want.
Now, you need to document their responsibilities and key metrics in what I call an Executive Performance Profile. This step, too, gets skipped or glossed over all the time, but it's essential.
At these meetings, ask each employee: “How likely are you to achieve these goals on time?” Notice we're asking for a prediction, not a progress report. This may seem subtle, but it's crucial.

If you let employees just feed you data, “Hey boss, I'm 10% done… 20% done… 50% done”, they're not taking accountability for delivering the result. They're just reporting progress, which means you're the one ultimately accountable.
There are good reasons a goal might not be achieved. But there are very few good reasons someone didn't know they weren't going to achieve it.

The main thing I want to communicate here is that so many managers (CEOs included) jump straight to the accountability conversation without laying this foundation. That's unfair to the employee and to the organization. … That works a hell of a lot better than hire → hope → retaliate.” Archived from Managing the Future on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Fred Rogers, the Teaching Mentor
q: While competitors ran animated features, Rogers stuck to physical sets and puppeteering. While “best practice” in children's television programming shifted to graphics and variety and speed and novelty, Rogers started every show walking onto the same old set and following the same old ritual: song, jacket, cardigan, shoes.
Too often, what we call “best practice” is really just “new” or “popularly accepted” or “endorsed by a guru.

The term “best practice” gets thrown around a lot, and it makes sense: we're all after “what's best for kids” and, therefore, we want to be doing the “best practices” possible for getting after that best. The trouble with this term, however, is that it's become over-extended.

Educators have got to have minds and hearts and souls that deeply understand how students work, how learning works, and how basic teacher moves can help students learn. With deep understanding in place, we're able to develop classrooms that look simple, even laughably so, like Rogers', yet produce consistent and profound results.
Good, timeless, well-founded practice > what passes as “best practice” these days.

Rogers seems to have been an expert at the internal work of teaching. The learning, the understanding, the processing. His clarity of thought, his obvious goodness, his simplicity of practice, his deep humility: these were the natural results of discipline and reflection, not luck or genetics or talent.

He understood himself. He understood his neighbor. He was a student of what it means to be a human being. (And no, not everyone is.) Such apprenticeship must be first intended and then sought; you don't accidentally stumble upon it.

Rogers knew he didn't control the circumstances of the world. He couldn't change the attention-hungry changes in children's programs. He just controlled his program, his teaching. He contented himself in that, worked at doing good through that for a full career, and his legacy speaks for itself.” Archived from Dave Stuart Jr. newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Close the Tabs: An End of Term Ritual for School Leaders
q: As the autumn term winds down and we head towards the Christmas break, school leaders often find themselves carrying far more than festive cheer into the holidays. We often carry open loops — the mental “tabs” that never seem to close.

It's strangely common: the people we line manage often get the least of our time. Urgent parent emails, safeguarding triage, assessment deadlines…these soak up the hours. Meanwhile, your competent, dependable team members quietly keep everything afloat.

Ah, the last-minute paperwork. The document you meant to submit. The file you intended to upload. The resource you promised to send “later today.” These are the things that wake us at 3am on Christmas Eve, demanding attention from the depths of our subconscious.” “You don't need to solve these before Christmas. But you do need to name them. Write each worry on a piece of paper, just the problem, not the solution. Allow it to live there instead of in your mind. Let the page hold it over Christmas so that your brain doesn't have to.
January can feel like a cold plunge if the first week back hasn't been thought about in advance.

At the end of a long term, patterns reveal themselves. Perhaps you've particularly noticed: rising stress, recurring disorganisation, a structural issue in your school, a creeping sense of overwhelm. So ask: What words, ideas or emotions do I want the New Year to hold?

It has been a long term. Students are tired. Behaviour dips. Emotions run high. And sometimes the things students say or do can sit heavy with us long after the moment has passed. But remember the mantra: They are the children. We are the adults.
Close the tabs you can. Write down the ones you can't, and walk into the holiday knowing you have earned every moment of rest.” Archived from Language for Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: AI Tools Are Ideal for Scenario Planning
q: Even the best laid plans can fail when leaders encounter situations they didn't expect.
Through Scenario Planning, leaders can account for a wide range of possible situations. They can pressure test their plans and make sure they aren't caught unaware or without a backup strategy.

Scenario Planning that provides a clear benefit has traditionally required deep research, robust dialogue, and intensive discussion of different possibilities by the organization's most talented people. But with the large language models of AI now available to leaders, scenario planning can be fast, inexpensive, and more thorough.
As leaders begin the planning process, they can ask LLMs to poke holes in it, to identify the underlying assumptions the strategy depends upon, and to reveal potential missteps.

Don't depend on a single prompt. When the LLM provides its output, push against it, probe the assumptions it makes, and dive deeper into the questions at hand. The most useful outputs seldom come in the model's first response.

By nature, LLMs are agreeable and seek to satisfy the user. When you're looking for critique, ask the model to be critical. Ask it to serve as a true red team partner, poking holes in every aspect of your plan.
LLMs produce volumes of ideas and content far beyond what would be reasonable to ask a human being. Don't limit yourself. Rather than ask for one idea, ask for 20.

Great Scenario Planning keeps human judgment at the center while using AI to accelerate the process and strengthen the output. As helpful as LLMs can be in researching, defining, and planning across scenarios, leaders need to decide which are worth their attention.” Archived from Admired Leadership Field Notes on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: 8 Bad Education Models
q: As we consider (or ignore) the opportunity to rethink and re-imagine education, all of our worst ideas about what education actually is have come bubbling to the surface like hippopotamus farts in a stagnant pond.

Students are just empty vessels, just a collection of inert, powerless, agency-free tubs into which teachers pour education like melted butter. It's important that the empty vessels hold still and avoid interfering with the process.” “Education is for turning out useful meat widgets who will be able to meet the needs of their future employers. The measure of whether or not something should be included in schooling is a simple question: would someone someday be willing to pay you for having this skill?

Students are just little machines, and teaching is just science and engineering. If you do steps A, B and C exactly as the science tells you to, every single student will learn exactly what they're supposed to learn. Variations in success are the result of teachers not following the instructions exactly.

Follow the data. Students generate it, teachers respond to it, and administrators crunch it while never leaving their offices. Do not be distracted by the human beings involved in this activity; they simply generate a bunch of noise that will distract you from the pure, clear data.

Like a taco or a toaster, education is just a consumer good and students and their families are just customers. The mission of schools is to produce just enough of the product of just enough quality at the lowest possible cost and the highest possible price.
Children are uncivilized little beasts and they have to be whipped into shape. Their every impulse must be tightly controlled, their behavior constantly monitored, and compliance regularly enforced.

Look, people are destined for different stations in life. Not everyone needs to learn how to be a leader or the chef or the boss; we need followers and order-takers and people who do the grunt work they're told to do. Education is part of the process of sorting students into their rightful place.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Grading Teacher Performance Kills Growth
q: When I started my teacher training over ten years ago, I faced a series of challenges like the relentless planning burden and subpar mentoring among them. But there was another element that amplified my anxiety to levels I haven’t fully recovered from: the lesson grading system.

A 60-minute snapshot of a teacher managing a highly complex concept with a challenging class is reduced to a single word. This grade carries zero context about the teacher’s long-term planning, their mastery of instructional atoms, or their relationships with the students.
When you grade, you ruin the positivity of the process and shift the focus from growth to judgment.
In too many schools, a mentor provides excellent, supportive, constructive feedback, but then ruins the entire process by adding a grade or a judgmental label.
It doesn’t matter if you stop using numbers and switch to kinder, less judgmental words. The act of assigning a label remains a negative judgment that breeds anxiety and defensiveness.

This transforms the observation from a performance review into a coaching session, making the process one of collaboration and development rather than anxiety and judgment.” Archived from Dr Emanuele on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: When a Team Member Doesn't Prioritize Your Priorities
q: Sometimes unknowingly and other times deliberately, team members can follow their own priorities and fail to follow yours. This can be a source of great frustration for leaders, as the work they want to get done takes a secondary position or, worse, gets ignored.
Leaders faced with the challenge of a team member who ignores their priorities are best served by initially NOT presuming bad intent.

It’s possible the team member has received competing priorities from other leaders; they are simply overloaded, and it only appears they are avoiding the priorities. Or, perhaps, they don’t understand the priority set.” “In the case where the root cause is not obvious to the team member, or they are unwilling to share it, the leader needs to make one point perfectly clear: the priorities they set are non-negotiable. This means the team member’s evaluation and success depend on their accomplishing them.
By connecting the priorities to the team’s vision, purpose, or long-range goals, the leader can further imprint the consequences of placing anything ahead of the priorities.

By plainly naming the refusal and avoiding any debate over the priorities, the leader must act decisively to define the role the team member is asked to play and to offer them a clear choice to accept the role or exit the team.
Effectiveness in anything is about doing the right things. Leaders set priorities to make the team more effective. If someone can’t or won’t align with those priorities, trust gets broken.
As author Jim Collins likes to say, “The moment you feel the need to tightly manage someone, you likely have the wrong person.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: So Much We Do, We Do Again (Resuscitating Repetition)
q: They say that writing is rewriting and that good reading is rereading. The wisdom we have inherited tells us again and again — or repeats for us — that anything mastered is done not once but many, many times.

Quintilian tells us, “It is better to learn a little thoroughly and to repeat it often, than to learn much superficially.” Jerome writes, “Constant repetition is the mother of studies” and Seneca says simply “let us repeat often what we have learned.

Rightly conceived, repetition is a very good and human thing. We employ it to learn, perform, and enjoy music; we learn it to dance, play tennis, and make a good old-fashioned. Children understand innately the virtue of repetition and even demand it: Read it again Daddy! One more time!

The root of this Latinate word is instructive — for it means to petition or seek…again. There are many good things to seek in life, worth seeking and finding over and over again, whether a great concert, a great drink, or a great book.

Of course there is a kind of repetition employed in education (and in other aspects of life) that merits the description “drill and kill” and “rote memory.” To seek again, to repeat, is deeply human and good thing. But anything good can be corrupted, and we corrupt the good of repetition repeatedly.

It is possible to review the causes for the Revolutionary War in a way that is dull and uninspiring (a regurgitation or retreading). Dull teachers do this regularly. But it is also possible to review (revisit, reconsider, remark, return, relive) the cause of the war in ways that are remarkable, refreshing, and renewing.
Much depends on which verb you wish to attach the sacred prefix.

Much of bad teaching is bad repetition that equates to test prep. Such repetition seeks nothing but a grade on a multiple choice test, making such instruction repulsive because the teacher merely rehashes content and reveals no new sight, no refreshing perspective.” Archived from Renewing Classical Education on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Combining Student Scores: Why Adding Subjects Is Trickier Than It Looks
q: One example that Paul shared with me really got me thinking about what happens when we add scores from different subjects.

If we have a group of 12 students, and have their percentage scores on 8 subjects, it might seem easy to work out who is the best students. We just add up the scores on each of the 8 subjects, and see who has the highest total.
However, there is a problem here. Subject 1 used most of the mark range, with scores ranging from 10 to 100, while others, such as subject 3, have scores ranging only from 40 to 60.
To control for this, we could replace scores with class ranks, giving the highest scoring student in each subject a rank of 1, and the lowest scoring student a rank of 12.
However, when we use ranks, we throw away information, because we take no account of how much better the first ranked student is than the lowest ranked student; the difference will always be 11.

Instead, a better approach might be to scale the scores so that every subject uses the full range of scores from 0 to 100, with the lowest scoring student getting 0, the highest scoring student getting 100, and the others scaled in between.
Now, the student who was top — Adams — is at the bottom, and the student who was at the bottom — Lant — is at the top.
If that doesn’t make you realize that adding up scores like this is not as straightforward as it seems, I don’t know what will.” Archived from Dylan Wiliam on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Case for Saying Less
q: When people don’t understand, explaining more usually makes it worse.
When someone looks confused, we assume the problem is a lack of explanation. That assumption is usually wrong. It’s a habit built over years of good intentions.

Controlled experiments in cognitive science point to a quieter truth. When researchers gave people additional explanations they believed would help, comprehension actually declined. Not slightly. Reliably.” “The issue wasn’t intelligence or motivation. It was capacity. Working memory is limited. When it’s flooded, the brain shifts from understanding to coping.
When unnecessary information is removed, understanding improves. People make better decisions because they can grasp the core more quickly.
This is why long explanations blur instead of clarify. It’s why meetings drift even when everyone means well, and why good ideas lose their edge the moment we over-defend them.
Clarity isn’t created by effort. It’s created by restraint.
You don’t need to say everything you know. You need to protect what matters most.” Archived from 1-Minute Wednesday (gregmckeown.com) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Is There Pressure, and What To Do About It
q: We’ve all been there. That crushing feeling of being squeezed from every direction. Stakeholders want faster delivery. Teams are confused about priorities. Leadership keeps asking for more updates while we’re already drowning in meetings.
Much of the pressure we feel comes from organizational patterns that we can actually change.

When direction is unclear, everything becomes a battle. Without clear direction, teams can’t move quickly because they’re constantly second-guessing themselves. This uncertainty creates bottlenecks everywhere.” “When trust is missing, organizations panic. They create layers of approval. Extra oversight. More checks and balances. This creates a vicious cycle. The lack of trust makes teams less effective, which then justifies even more oversight.

People schedule meetings because they’re scared. Scared of missing something important. Scared they don’t have enough information to do their jobs properly. Before you know it, your calendar is packed.

Build trust through radical transparency. Share your planning process openly. When problems arise, bring them up before others discover them. Admitting problems early makes people trust you more, not less.

Push decision-making down. Create frameworks. Write down decision criteria. Give your team the tools to make good choices without checking with you first. The goal isn’t losing control. It’s creating systems that work even when you’re not directly involved.

The most effective product leaders aren’t those who thrive under constant pressure. They’re the ones who build organizations where good work can happen without that pressure in the first place.” Archived from Leading in Product on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Whole Books and Slow School
q: We don’t read whole books in school nearly as much as we used to, and that’s not an accident. It’s a design choice baked into the standards and testing regime we’ve built.

Common Core treated reading as a skill rather than a practice: a transferable ability that could be exercised on any passage. If that’s true, any passage will do, and short passages are cheaper to write, align, and test.

A whole book does things an excerpt cannot. It lets a character develop. It lets a reader live inside a world for weeks. It trains the attention span that short-passage reading is quietly eroding.” “The classroom conversation that a whole book supports is fundamentally different from the conversation a packet of excerpts supports. In one, everyone shares a world; in the other, everyone shares a few sentences.

The argument is not that every class must read the same canonical novel in the same way. The argument is that the experience of reading a whole book, with other people who have read the whole book, is worth preserving.

Slow school is a broader principle. Mathematics benefits from time with a hard problem. History benefits from time inside a long source. Writing benefits from a draft that matures across weeks rather than periods.

The assumption that faster is better, that more units covered means more learning, is doing a lot of damage. It drives schools toward the excerptable and the measurable and away from the experiences that actually make educated people.

Protecting time is an act of resistance in a system built for speed. Put the whole book back on the desk. Give students the chance to live with it.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Undemocratic School Primer
q: There are many ways to divide up the sides of the education debates. One is between those who believe in civic democratic ideals and those who do not.

Premise 1: All human beings have equal worth and are equally deserving of autonomy, opportunity, power, and privilege. Under this premise, the school system would exist to provide opportunity to all students.

Premise 2: Some human beings have more value than others, and are more deserving of autonomy, power, and privilege. In that world, schools exist not for uplift, but for sorting, to help everyone find and settle happily into their proper place.

Betters may learn arts and culture and what we think of as a broad liberal education. But future meat widgets need to learn marketable skills, job skills that will make them useful to their future corporate-boss Betters.

For Lessers, obedience and compliance are important. Schools are supposed to reinforce that message, reminding students that they are under the sole and complete control of their parents and must never, ever question that control.

It’s not always easy to talk through the issues with them because some of the words have different meanings; we can all say that every child should get the education they deserve or that is best suited to them, but we mean different things.
Nor are all school choice fans bettersists. I’m not even sure that some school choice fans really understand who they’ve teamed up with.

Betterists pose a real challenge to any sort of discussion or debate about education in this country, because they hold a fundamentally different view of the purpose of education, a profoundly different idea about how the country is supposed to work.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Influence of Speed in Relationships
q: Something simple and powerful happens in the first seconds of a conversation. Whether the exchange turns productive or not is often decided before the substance is even on the table.

Validating another person early and quickly in a conversation changes the trajectory of the exchange. Not agreement. Not flattery. A brief, genuine acknowledgement of what the other person is doing, feeling, or trying to accomplish.

The mechanism is social, not linguistic. Early validation signals that you are in the exchange with the other person rather than across the table from them, and that signal is registered before the content has been parsed.” “Leaders who default to evaluation — let me assess this proposal — get less truthful information and less willingness to iterate. Leaders who default to validation get better input and a team that surfaces problems earlier.
Validation is not agreement. It is recognition. It says: I see what you are trying to do, and I am here with you in the attempt. Whether I end up agreeing with you is a later question.

Notice the first sentence you say when a direct report brings you a problem. If it is an evaluation, a redirection, or an objection, the conversation is already narrowed. If it is a brief validation, the conversation is open.
The discipline is not to pretend to agree. It is to slow down for two seconds, acknowledge what the person is attempting, and then disagree if disagreement is warranted.
The shift is small, and the cumulative effect across a team is large. Speed in validation is one of the quiet multipliers of leadership.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Professional Scepticism
q: Until education becomes the kind of profession that reveres evidence, we should not be surprised to find its experts dispensing unproven methods, endlessly flitting from one fad to another. The greatest victims of these fads are the very students who are most at risk.
Science can help us understand what is. It is far less helpful when it comes to deciding what ought to be. Facts about the world do not contain values hidden inside them, waiting to be discovered.

To be professional sceptical is to engage in the disciplined habit of questioning claims by asking what evidence supports them, how that evidence was generated, and what would count against the claim being true.

We are not neutral judges of our own ideas. We are inclined to defend beliefs we have invested time, effort or reputation in. We discount evidence that challenges us and overvalue evidence that confirms what we already think.

The aim of research should not be to prove ourselves right but to find out where we are wrong. Randomised controlled trials, laboratory experiments and meta analyses matter because they are designed to falsify claims, not to endorse them.
Scepticism must cut both ways: it should guard us against premature rejection as well as premature adoption.
Every untested claim adopted in good faith carries an opportunity cost. Time spent on ineffective practice is time not spent on something better.

If teaching is to rise above the level of homeopathy, professional scepticism has to be seen as an ethical obligation rather than an optional extra. Children deserve more than confidence and conviction.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Onions: What Understanding Actually Means
q: What do we mean when we say a pupil “understands” something? The word is doing an astonishing amount of work in classrooms, and most of the time we don’t notice that it is.

Take five numbers, any five numbers. Arrange them in a 5×5 grid following a simple rule. Every row, every column, and both diagonals will sum to five times the middle number. That’s the trick. But what does it mean to “understand” it?

A pupil who can follow the procedure and produce the grid understands something. A pupil who can explain why every row, column, and diagonal sums to five times the centre understands something more.” “A pupil who can prove it, generalise it to n×n, and design a related puzzle from scratch has peeled another layer. These are not the same achievement, but we call them all “understanding.
The classroom consequence is that “Do you understand?” is a near-useless question, because teacher and pupil can answer it honestly while meaning completely different things.

The questions we ask, in the moment and on assessments, are what actually anchor our claim about what a pupil knows. A fluent procedure can hide an absent explanation; an absent explanation will trip them up later.

The most humbling moment in any teacher’s career is discovering that something you thought you understood has a layer you had never noticed. Good teaching is, in part, building habits that make that discovery routine rather than rare.

Understanding, like an onion, has layers. Our job is to know which layer we are asking about, which layer we are teaching to, and which layer our pupils are actually operating in.” Archived from Dylan Wiliam on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Most Germans Want Minimum Age for Social Media
a: Katharina Wedel, Larissa Zierow, and colleagues
q: An overwhelming majority of German adults — 85 percent — support a minimum age of 16 years for using social media. This is the finding of the latest ifo Education Survey.

What is perhaps even more striking is that 47 percent of adolescents themselves support a minimum age of 16 for social media use. Nearly half of the population that would be affected by such a rule says, in effect, “yes, we would welcome this.

These results land in a specific policy moment. Germany is debating whether to follow Australia’s lead in setting a legal minimum age for social media, and this survey provides the clearest evidence yet of broad public support for such a move.” “The survey adds to the growing cross-national case that adolescent social media saturation is not a narrow mental health problem but a developmental problem, and that policy tools of the kind Australia has pioneered have much wider public backing than the debate often assumes.

When nearly half of adolescents themselves say they would welcome a delay in access, the standard objection that age limits are paternalistic becomes much harder to sustain. Teens, not just parents, are telling the survey they see the harm.

The political window for a phone-free childhood, longer than many policymakers have assumed, is open. What the survey shows is that the public, and crucially a large share of the affected age group, is ready.

These findings should sharpen the case for action. Germany, like Australia, can move from debate to legislation, and it can do so knowing that the evidence of public support is no longer thin or speculative.

Delaying social media access until 16 is not just a parental preference. It is a position a near-majority of adolescents themselves endorse, and an overwhelming majority of adults share.” Archived from After Babel (Jonathan Haidt newsletter) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How I Trained My Memory, and What It Taught Me About Learning
q: I spent several months training myself to memorise 100 random digits in five minutes. It worked. I can now do it, most days. But the interesting thing is not the result. The interesting thing is what the training revealed about how learning works.

The headline skill — memorise 100 digits in 5 minutes — is emergent. It’s made up of component skills you practise separately, the way a pianist practises scales, chord shifts, and sight-reading before ever playing a piece.
Small chunks beat large ones. Every time I tried to process more than a few digits at a time, my accuracy collapsed. Every time I stuck to the two-digit chunk the PAO system uses, I was fine.
The connection is everything. The vivid, often absurd story linking one image to the next is what makes retrieval possible at speed. A bland connection is a broken connection.
Varied practice beat repetitive practice. The days I mixed in different digit sequences, different starting points, different distractions, I got better faster than the days I drilled the same thing.

Effortful retrieval is where the durable learning lives. The moment a recall felt easy, I was usually about to get it wrong the next time. The moment it felt hard, I was usually about to strengthen it.

Distraction has a measurable cost. I could see it in my own timings, reliably, before I could feel it subjectively. Five seconds of checking a phone cost me ten seconds of recall speed on the next attempt.

Transfer is narrower than it feels. Getting better at memorising digits did not make me better at remembering names, or facts in a meeting. Transfer is a skill you have to build on purpose; it does not come free with practice.” Archived from fivetwelvethirteen on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Got Regrets Yet? Teachers and the Four Types of Regret
q: Regret isn’t just a rumination. Used well, it’s a source of information. It tells us what we value, what we wish we had done differently, and, most usefully, what we want to do now.
Dan Pink, in his book The Power of Regret, identifies four types of regret that cut across cultures: Foundation regrets, Boldness regrets, Moral regrets, and Connection regrets.

Foundation regrets come from failing to do the slow, unglamorous work that sets a person up for long-term flourishing. For teachers, this often looks like systems not built, habits not formed, subject expertise not deepened.

Boldness regrets come from playing it safe when a braver choice was available. For teachers, this might mean the unit we didn’t try, the discussion we chickened out of, the project we shrank to fit our comfort zone.
Moral regrets come from moments when we acted against our values, even briefly. A sharp word to a struggling student, a rushed judgment in a parent email, a corner cut on a colleague who needed us.

Connection regrets come from relationships left unattended. The student we never quite got through to, the co-worker we meant to thank, the kid who slipped through the cracks while we were busy with the louder ones.
Pink offers a simple three-step process: relive the regret briefly, reframe it as information about what you value, then extract and apply a single concrete change.

Our regrets, handled well, become the coordinates for the next chapter. They point us toward the Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging we most want to build next.” Archived from Dave Stuart Jr. on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

q: The Bannister Effect, in general, is what happens when one person breaks a mental barrier, and suddenly everyone else can too.

t: Research Bite 49: Teacher Judgment Accuracy of Student Well-Being
q: If teachers remember one thing from this study, it should be that their judgments of students’ subjective well-being are only low to moderate in accuracy.

Overall, our findings point to a nuanced role of student behaviours and teacher-student relationships in shaping teachers’ judgments of students’ subjective well-being
Raising awareness about these factors and the importance of subjective well-being is crucial for adaptive teaching.

t: Authority Isn't Power
q: The CEO has authority. The executive assistant has power. Most people can't tell the difference.
Authority is the ability to make decisions. Power is the ability to determine which decisions get made. Authority is visible on the org chart. Power is invisible until you need it.

You spend eighteen months trying to reach a CEO you want to partner with. Cold emails. LinkedIn messages. Mutual connections. Zero response. Your colleague gets a meeting with the same person in two weeks.

t: The Long-Term Memory Problem: Why Teaching and Learning Policies Fail
q: Leaders tell me that they think the policy is good and that teachers are following it, but student outcomes don't seem to be improving, and they aren't sure why.” “It seems to be a smooth operation, with well-written policies, effective staff training, and a positive culture around professional and institutional growth. Unfortunately, the bottom line is the bottom line, and if we aren't shifting the dial on student outcomes, then however lovely our school is, something is clearly going wrong.

However well designed our lessons, however clear our explanations, however thorough our checks for understanding and however extensive our independent practice: without a clear strategy for how students are going to remember it over the long term, we are wasting our time.

In order to strengthen our students' long-term memory, we need to give them lots of opportunities to retrieve and practise their knowledge. These opportunities need to not only be extensive, but also to be appropriately spaced and spread out over time.

Professor Coe's seminal work on 'proxies for learning' taught us that when trying to establish the quality of a teacher or lesson we latch onto things that are readily observable, like student behaviour, busy-ness, and if feedback is being delivered. Whether students are learning over the long term feels more ephemeral.

Asking students questions about things you taught them and discovering that they remember nothing is difficult and frustrating, and most of us will consciously or subconsciously try to avoid getting into that situation.
When teachers 'set and forget' they therefore communicate that they don't really care what students do, so long as they do it. But if the teacher doesn't care, the students certainly won't.

If we have not adequately strategised for long-term learning, nothing we do in the class can compensate. We need to scrutinise our teaching and our leading and wonder: have we been looking in the wrong direction?” Archived from Carousel on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Self-Confidence Is Shaped by the People Whose Validation and Respect We Seek

people with a strong external anchor experience lower well-being, higher anxiety, more mood swings, less intrinsic motivation, and more emotional volatility.
when a person’s sense of self-worth becomes too contingent on forces they don’t influence or control, their self-esteem and self-confidence can fluctuate wildly.

t: Self-Confidence Is Shaped by the People Whose Validation and Respect We Seek
q: People have a fundamental need to seek the attention of others and to be respected and admired for who they are and what they do. All people and in every culture. The only critical difference between people is the source of this attention.” “Some people anchor their self-worth and self-identity externally rather than internally. For those externally focused, the internet and social media offer fast and abundant signals that satisfy their need for positive feedback about themselves.

Because the relevance of the audience is less important to those externally anchored, they prioritize scale, visibility, and reach. Approval from large audiences feels validating, even if the individual opinions are shallow or lack context.

Internally anchored people, on the other hand, have a more stable sense of self and rely mostly on feedback from trusted friends and colleagues or from others who have the expertise to calibrate their value.

When the internal anchor is extremely high, people will actively avoid social proof or attention that doesn't come from those they know or from those they deem worthy of respecting them, so they distance themselves from social media and other forms of large audience acknowledgement and feedback.
Predictably, people with a strong external anchor experience lower well-being, higher anxiety, more mood swings, less intrinsic motivation, and more emotional volatility.

Research also confirms that seeking attention and validation from strangers can produce an overreaction to criticism, more defensive behavior, a rumination over negative feedback, and a higher fear of missing out.

If you notice a team or family member's self-confidence swings widely over the course of days or weeks without any apparent reason, it may be that they have increased their need for validation by anchoring it externally, through social media or other forms.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Positive Framing, Part 1: Live in the Now
a: The Teach Like a Champion Team
q: For many teachers, this coming week can be one of the trickiest of the year. Students are excited for winter break, the energy in the room is shifting, and attention can feel elastic.
When classes feel wiggly, it's easy to focus on what just went wrong. We've talked about this. Why aren't you on page 12? But looking backward rarely gets students (or us) where we need to go.

Live in the Now shifts the frame away from the misstep and toward what should happen next. It's forward-facing, actionable, and motivating.” “The core move is simple: give the smallest, clearest step toward success. Instead of 'You should be taking notes,' try something like: 'Pencil in hand, ready to capture this next example.

Students respond to specific, bite-sized directions, especially during high-energy weeks. Clear next steps reduce resistance, refocus attention, and communicate our belief in their ability to follow through.
When you describe the positive next action, rather than the mistake, you change the story students see. Great coaching is about always describing what you want to see next.
No frustration. No backward-looking critique. Just clear, doable next steps. And because the direction is specific, students know exactly how to be successful right now.

Positive Framing works because it preserves trust. Even small choices in phrasing, especially during potentially messy weeks, signal belief: You can do this. I'm here to help you get there.” Archived from Teach Like a Champion on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: When to Form a Task Force to Address a Problem
q: Some problems require a unique organizing scheme. One that allows leaders to apply singular focus and commitment to a complex or difficult problem.

Typically referred to as a Task Force, the idea is to assemble a group of highly skilled team members who will work together to aggressively address a problem until it is resolved. Once the task is completed, the group disbands.” “When an issue involves urgency, complexity, and exceeds the demands of the regular team, leaders turn to these temporary work groups to make headway quickly and to provide the rapid action and intensity that thorny problems require for resolution.

Most team members do so enthusiastically because the request to serve on a Task Force is viewed as a recognition of their expertise and offers a pathway to make an even bigger contribution to the team’s success.

Task Forces handle temporary, mission-specific goals and one-off events or problems with urgency, while Committees represent diverse viewpoints and are expected to examine all options and deliberately decide on the best one.

Interestingly, organizations with a tradition of establishing Committees rarely use Task Forces to increase speed, urgency, and action. They generally prefer not to distinguish between experts or to elevate one problem over others.

Committees still excel in sustained roles such as risk management, compensation, and policymaking, where institutional knowledge helps to drive accountability. But organizations that are too Committee-focused often give up the agility and speed in decision-making that allows them to compete.

Mixing the use of Task Forces and Committees allows an organization to maintain the oversight it desires with the agility and speed in decision-making it needs to compete.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: A Seat at the Table: Knowledge, Inheritance, and the Purpose of Schooling
q: For some, it has somehow come to mean rote memorisation, silent classrooms and pupils treated as passive containers for information. For others, it signals centralised curriculum packages, compliance masquerading as rigour and the belief that learning is distilled to the delivery and testing of facts, facts and more facts.
At its core, a knowledge-rich curriculum is not a claim about how much pupils know, but about what knowledge does. It begins from a view of thinking as something that depends on what is known.
Without it, analysis becomes opinion dressed as insight, creativity collapses into improvisation without constraint, and critical thinking degenerates into reflexive conspiracy theory generation.

As Christine Counsell has argued, curriculum is a promise made to future teachers. It is a commitment about what we believe young people will need in order to understand the world they are entering, not just cope with the next assessment.

There have been “lethal mutations”, cases where poor implementation reduced curriculum to rote learning and stripped teachers of agency, turning curriculum into something “done to” them rather than “done with” them.
The collection insists that subjects are not interchangeable delivery systems but distinct intellectual traditions, each with its own criteria for explanation, argument and evidence.
As Dylan Wiliam argues, “If exams were abolished tomorrow, advocates would still believe in a knowledge-rich approach as the right thing to do”. The reason is democratic.

Knowledge-rich intent too often meets skills-poor enactment. The result is frustration mistaken for high standards. If knowledge is to be genuinely empowering, the means of expressing it must be taught with the same care as the content itself.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: When Assessment Becomes a Conversation
a: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning
q: What we’re really interested in exploring is how Viva enables a more direct, spoken form of assessment—at scale. This isn’t about replacing written work, but about revealing layers of understanding that written artifacts alone often fail to show.

There’s a noticeable shift in posture and attention: students become more alert, more present, and more engaged with their own thinking. The format can feel slightly intimidating at first—yet that discomfort is part of what makes it valuable.” “It asks students to take ownership of their ideas in real time, rather than relying on distance, polish, or revision. And in the AI era, this sort of just-in-time conversational competency has real value.
Oral assessments surface whether students can explain, connect, and reason with ideas—not just reproduce them. They make understanding visible in ways written work often cannot.

What interests us about Viva is that it meaningfully changes this constraint. By structuring and scaling the questioning process, it makes oral assessment possible in contexts where it has traditionally been out of reach—not as a replacement for teacher judgment, but as a way to make those judgments more informed and more feasible.

Viva doesn’t function primarily as a safeguard; it functions more as a speed bump to generating one’s work with AI assistance. Because students must explain ideas aloud, in real time, and in response to questions generated directly from their own writing, the assessment shifts from product to process.
Oral assessment introduces real questions about access and fairness: how it intersects with anxiety, language processing, neurodiversity, and the accommodations many students understandably rely on.

We’re not treating Viva as a finished solution. We’re treating it as a design space: a chance to figure out how oral explanation can become a fair, repeatable part of how students demonstrate understanding.” Archived from Episcopal Academy CTL (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: This year in the science of learning
q: I sent 71 newsletters, conducted 11 video/podcast interviews, wrote seven Tools for Practice posts with the help of very smart educators, hosted one summer reader book club (a blast) and one live Q&A with readers and Paul Kirschner, a giant in the science of learning.” “I launched the Science of Learning Tracker, which is going to give readers an idea of where the science of learning is being implemented, whether it’s states, universities, districts or schools.

t: This Science-Backed Life Trap Is Why You're Stuck
q: The 3/10 job. The 3/10 relationship. The 3/10 life. Those break you open. They force change with the intensity of the negative experience. You hit the threshold of pain that activates every psychological and behavioral mechanism you have.

But the 6/10? That's the trap of good enough. It's not painful enough to trigger action. So you drift. You tolerate. You wait. You stay in jobs you've outgrown. In relationships that don't nourish. In routines that feel hollow.

The worst thing in the world isn't being on a bad path. The worst thing in the world is being on a good path that isn't yours. The bad path screams for change. The good path that isn't yours sits in silence.
The Region-Beta Paradox reminds us of the dangers of good enough. It takes courage to escape the trap. You have to force action. You have to choose uncertainty over comfort.
Courage isn't courageous because it works out. Courage is courageous because you act without knowing that it will.” Archived from sahilbloom.com on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Stop Adding & Start Improving
q: Essentially, it’s this myth that if teachers already do something well enough, there’s no point doing any further professional learning on this topic. But what if we’re missing the point of professional learning as a whole?
Expertise does not exempt us from learning. If anything, it increases our responsibility to keep refining.

The problem is, even for topics that do yield greater progress for students or are effective in achieving their aims, expertise doesn’t sufficiently development from tasting. Instead, it develops from returning to the same practice time and time again, applying it consistently and seeking feedback.

Implementation needs to be staged, and moving from initial exploration to implementation with fidelity on a particular technique can take years. Despite this, it isn't uncommon for schools to abandon an initiative after a term.

This drives a cycle of what is really novelty addiction and a prioritisation of visibility over depth. In doing so, leaders, albeit unintentionally, undermine the expertise of their teachers and the entire professional learning process.

Schools that make real impact aren’t about chasing novelty. They double down on what works and refuse to move until it has teeth. Their staff review the same principles time and time again with a focus on doing them better.

As someone working directly in the professional learning space, my biggest learning here is that professional learning isn’t so much about ticking off exposure to new ideas as it is about insisting on improvement. It’s not about doing more. It’s about doing better.

t: Prediction Accuracy at Key Stage 4
q: In total, 740 of our participating schools submitted both predicted grades and results. Overall, our dataset contains around 1 million predicted-actual grade pairs for 140 thousand pupils.

For these reasons, we don’t claim to be able to definitively answer a question like “how accurately can teachers predict attainment?” Instead, we’ll explore the more limited question “to what extent do the predicted grades made by teachers match their pupils’ results?

Computer science was the subject with the biggest difference in average grade, with predictions 0.4 grades higher than results, on average. There were four subjects where the difference in average grade between predictions and results rounds to zero.
English literature, despite having almost no difference between average predicted grades and results has one of the lowest percentages of predictions matching results, 34%.
Maths and the three art and design subjects are the only ones where more than 50% of predictions matched results.

Overall, most subjects are quite similar to each other in terms of average predicted grades vs results, with almost all subjects seeing differences of a quarter of a grade or less. There is more variation between subjects, however, when looking at the percentage of predictions which matched results.
Together, this implies that, nationally at least, predicted grades tend to match results quite closely at the cohort-level, but not at the pupil-level.

t: Our Children, Our Future: Tackling Child Poverty

The Child Poverty Strategy is an acknowledgement that schools cannot do it all. It belongs to the whole of society. It belongs to every department of government and every layer of policy.

t: Missing the Wood for the Trees
q: The claim that domain-adjacent prior knowledge does not support new in-domain learning looks, at first glance, like a body-blow to one of the most widely quoted maxims in educational psychology. If “the most important factor in learning is what students already know,” how can a new experimental study report that supplying domain-related knowledge makes no difference at all?

If this looks uncannily like the result reported by Buchin and Mulligan, that’s because both studies hinge on the same conceptual mistake. They assume that any increase in knowledge should automatically produce gains on any chosen assessment.

In both studies the same problem recurs: students were assessed on tasks that did not depend on the knowledge they had been taught. When the conceptual bridge between content and assessment is missing, null effects are almost guaranteed.

Predictive processing does not explain the failure of either study so much as re-describe it in more elaborate terms. The moment we abandon the assumption that the researchers actually supplied the prior knowledge the target task depended on, the puzzle evaporates. The flaw is methodological, not metaphysical.
Prior knowledge supports learning only when ideas genuinely interlock. It is the structure of the content, not the thematic label, that determines what counts as a prerequisite.

If a child cannot ride a bike because they cannot balance, no one suggests giving them a rocking horse and hoping the skill will emerge. And yet, when we step into academic domains, the clarity sometimes evaporates. A student who struggles to infer meaning from a passage in history is often given yet more historical facts, as if additional detail about the Battle of Hastings will compensate for not understanding how inference works.

We get distracted by domain labels and thematic proximity; we assume that because ideas sit near each other conceptually, one must support the other. Without the intuitive scaffolding of everyday contexts, we lose our grip on what is prerequisite and what is merely adjacent.

The most important factor in learning remains what students already know, provided that what they already know belongs to the structure of the new idea. Everything else, however close it might appear, is wood mistaken for trees.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Leaders Quickly Reframe Negative Promotion Decisions
q: Team members who expect to be promoted and learn that they have been turned down can be crestfallen. The disappointment after being rejected for promotion often creates despair, upset, and anguish.

No one likes to be jilted, but being turned down for promotion stings a little bit more than other rejections. That’s because negative promotion decisions can feel like a public verdict on the team member’s future.
Because the decision connects to core psychological needs like status, belonging, and self-esteem, the brain often treats it similarly to physical pain.
False promises, positive remarks, and validating comments don’t typically offer any relief.
Leaders can’t let the frame that the team members use shape the conversation. Team members hear the rejection as a declaration that they are not good enough.
When the leader believes this decision is temporary, the words “Not Yet” suggest a confidence that it is only a matter of time before they reach their goal of promotion.
Going backward and offering an account or justification solidifies hard feelings. Going forward and plotting the action for progress makes the conversation a catalyst for improvement.

Good leaders don’t allow people to wallow in disappointment if they can avoid it. They reframe the rejection as temporary and quickly move to what can be done to address it. Nothing ventilates the mind like a plan of action.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Creating people
q: The individual in contemporary society is not so much described by tests as constructed by them (Allan Hanson, 1994)

Every time we share the results of an assessment with pupils, we add a drop in the ocean of who they believe themselves to be. We often think of testing pupils as merely a means to ascertain what they know, but we rarely stop to think how the very act also shapes their self-concept.” “These micro-exposures provide us with repeated signals about how competent we are, how we compare to others, and what we may be worthy of achieving in the future.

The form in which results are conveyed may signal to pupils what the teacher (or the school or world more widely) believes about them - that they are a ‘failure’, exceeding or falling below expectations, or high/mediocre/low performing. Pupils can internalise the form so deeply that they even begin to describe themselves in these terms: “I am a level 4” or “I’m an epic failure at maths”.

It is this effect that leads pupils to say that they would rather be at the top of set 2 in maths than at the bottom of set 1. They know that it is not so much how well they perform, but how they feel about this performance as a result of the performance of those around them.

Whether we mean to or not, educators equate success at school with moral worth. I chose not to fight the system but to play with it. I did what I had to do to achieve my goals, I played the game, if you will. (Ruth Borland in The Irish Times, 27 September 2005)

But this, I think, is the crux of it: belonging is buoyed on a sea of noticing. And this sea of noticing helps belonging to take anchor, float, and set sail. To belong is to feel noticed. To feel seen. To feel valued. To feel respected.

Just as Adam Boxer says, “What does it say about us if we don’t hear their voices? If they can sit in front of us for an hour, and we barely recognise or register their existence? That their thoughts and opinions are excluded from our classroom conversation?

As teachers, we notice all the time. We are experts in noticing: that Jen still can’t quite grasp that thesis statement; that Chris has been late to school twice that week; that Zeynab has cuts on her arm; that Nat is bouncing his knee up and down after that assembly.
Pastoral noticing helps to forge the anchor of belonging; academic noticing helps belonging set sail.

t: Are Your People Trained Or Enabled?
q: Organizations invest billions annually in developing their workforce, yet many struggle to translate learning investments into durable performance improvements. At the heart of this challenge rests a fundamental distinction that is often overlooked: the difference between training your people and enabling your people.

Good training asks the question: “What do people need to know and understand to be able to do their jobs more effectively?” It operates on a push model. The organization decides what, when, and how learning happens.

Enablement, by contrast, is continuous and context-embedded. It requires an ecosystem of resources, tools, processes, and support systems that help people perform effectively in their daily workflows. Enablement asks: “What do people need to succeed, and how can we provide it when they need it?
I tend to think of training like an fancy appetizer at an overpriced restaurant. I mean, we kind of need it to get going, but it’s not nearly enough to satisfy and sustain us.
The distinction between training and enablement matters not just because people want and need support in the moment, but because knowledge transfer alone rarely produces lasting behavioral change.

Training and learning industry professionals generally agree that learners are likely to forget approximately 70% of training content within 24 hours and up to 90% within a week. This is supported by the concept of the forgetting curve, first documented by psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, which shows that without reinforcement, memory retention decays.

Training can promote dependency and even disempowerment, as people are adapted to leaning into a particular kind of person or setting for learning rather than seek it out in everyday moments. Enablement, on the other hand, empowers people to solve problems with greater autonomy.

The question isn’t whether to invest in training or enablement, but rather how to build enablement infrastructure that multiplies training’s impact and creates self-sustaining cultures of continuous learning and growth.” Archived from Honest Office (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
